The words

Blest is the man who fears the Lord!
His well established mind,
In every varying scene of life,
Shall true composure find.

Oft through the deep and stormy sea
The heavenly footsteps lie;
But on a glorious world beyond
His faith can fix its eye.

Though dark his present prospects be,
And sorrows round him dwell,
Yet hope can whisper to his soul,
That all shall issue well.

Full in the presence of his God,
Through every scene he goes;
And, fearing him, no other fear
His steadfast bosom knows.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Eb and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on s (B♭), on the word “Blest”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

These words were printed without an author's name in Hymns for Christian Devotion, compiled by John G. Adams and Edwin H. Chapin (Boston, 1846), as hymn 410 of its twenty-second edition (1853), “The Influence of Habitual Piety”, where the book credits them to the Exeter Collection.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Common Metre (8.6.8.6), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to ST. PETER; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Music (1826): Alexander R. Reinagle (died undefined)

Questions about Blest Is the Man Who Fears the Lord

What is the doh of Blest Is the Man Who Fears the Lord?

In this version, in Eb major, doh is Eb. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Blest Is the Man Who Fears the Lord start on?

It starts on s (B♭ in Eb major), a pickup on the word “Blest” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to s.

Is Blest Is the Man Who Fears the Lord in the public domain?

Yes. Alexander R. Reinagle died in undefined; the words were in print by 1853 and the music in 1826. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
